speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege, and since it is a matter of great personal concern, I have written down

what I intend to say. Yesterday, before, the public accounts committee, at Quebec, my integrity was called in question by the prime minister of my province, as reported by several Canadian newspapers.
Taking for granted that the report published in La Presse of April 5th page 25, is an accurate statement of what occurred in the public accounts committee, which report was moreover substantially corroborated by all other Quebec newspapers, I notice the following words:
Hon. Mr. Duplessis:	Do you know Mr. Edouard Lacroix, the federal member for Beauce?
Mr. Gagnon:	xes sir.
Hon. Mr. Duplessis:	He is a lumber merchant ?
Mr. Gagnon:	Yes sir.
Hon. Mr. Duplessis: Tell the committee what you know about Mr. Lacroix's dealings.
Mr. Gagnon: Under a statute of 1910, it was forbidden to export to the United States any lumber coming from crown lands. Well, in 1924-25, Mr. Lacroix cut down several thousand feet of lumber which he shipped to the United States.
Hon. Mr. Duplessis: Where was that timber cut?
Mr. Gagnon:	On crown lands in Daaquam
township.
In reply to this first charge, I wish to state that contrary to what the prime minister of Quebec endeavoured to bring out according to -what I have quoted, never, -absolutely never has a single cord of wood from Daaquam township been exported to the United States either by myself or by any of my companies. So much with regard to that first malicious or politically sadistic falsehood.
Then the same individual further tried to show through a man in his pay that I had cut trees of a smaller size than that provided in the statute, in that same Daaquam township, and therefore that I owed $117,991 in fines to the provincial government. Well, Mr. Speaker, I hold in my hand a receipt from the government of the province of Quebec, showing that all the fines that I have incurred during the whole course of my life through regular development of our forests, and over which I had no personal or absolute control, amounted not to SI 17,991, as erroneously and maliciously stated by Mr. Duplessis, but actually to only $5,000.
Not only can I say and prove to the people that the offences to which I have referred were the only ones committed, but I have also before me all the proper receipts from the provincial government showing conclusively that I owe nothing, and moreover that I always paid regularly each year and in proper

Privilege-Mr. Lacroix
time the amounts which I was bound to pay under the law. And these amounts are not those which Mr. Duplessis also tried viciously to establish; I have paid $121,910.90 in excess of that, namely $244,601.98.
Mr. Speaker, if I am wearying the house with these personal details, it is not so much for me as for the sake of my wife and children of whom I may well be proud, unlike Mr. Duplessis, and to whom I shall leave the well known reputation of an honest business man, who always paid fair salaries to his employees, thus giving my family an example of Christian charity, of honesty and of morality which I would be loath to compare with that of the prime minister of the province of Quebec, whatever he may say.
In fact, if the prime minister had been prompted by that spirit of justice which must always be based on Christian charity, he would not have singled out the member for Beauce in connection with the logging operations in Daaquam township; he would have also referred to previous and later companies-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite apparent, I think, without going into the authorities at all, that it is competent for any hon. member who has been attacked in his capacity as a member of this house to rise in his place on a question of privilege and make
such explanation or statement as he may think desirable to negative the inferences to be drawn from any public statement attacking his honour or his fitness as a member of the house. But to rise in his place and discuss his relations with the provincial government with respect to lumber transactions and licences for the cutting of timber is to deal with purely a provincial matter, and if we are to listen for a quarter of an hour on a question of privilege to a statement that has to do with purely a provincial matter, where are we going to land? That is the question at issue.
I cannot but think that the hon. member will realize that he is dealing with something that might properly be dealt with in the legislature at Quebec, something having to do with his capacity as a business man, not as a member of this chamber, and the discharge of his obligations in connection with a matter affecting timber licences and timber rights in that province, over which we have no control. If every transaction that affects the question of a man's relations to provincial governments or to contractual obligations with respect to timber or sales of lumber in the United States is to become the subject matter of discussion in this chamber on a question of privilege, certainly, Mr. Speaker, this house is going to be in rather a difficult position.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few years ago, when a committee sitting in Manitoba had found something against a member of this house, the late Hon. Mr. Rogers, I well remember that he rose in his place in this house and answered the charges that had been made against him, not as a member of the House of Commons but as a public man in the province of Manitoba.
As far as my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) is concerned, I listened to what he was saying. He was grossly attacked yesterday, not as a member of the House of Commons but as a man, and he takes the opportunity to defend himself and his honour in the only tribunal of which he is a member, namely, the House of Commons.
My right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) may be right in saying that the hon. member should defend himself in the legislature or committee of the legislature of Quebec, but if my right hon. friend knew how proceedings are being conducted there, he would know that men are attacked and are not given the right to say even one word in their defence or in explanation of the charges made against them.
I merely want to add that all of the colleagues of the member for Beauce ought to support him in his endeavour to vindicate his honour as a man.
Privilege-Mr. Lacroix

maintopic: PRESS REPORTS OP STATEMENTS MADE BEFORE THE PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE OF THE QUEBEC LEGISLATURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have one observation to make with reference to what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has just said. I prefaced my observations by the remark that any statement made outside of this house that reflects upon the honour or fitness of a member to sit in this chamber as a representative of the people, he is within his rights in denying as a matter of privilege. He has the right to deny any insult directed against him outside of this chamber touching his capacity as a member; indeed his duty is to deal with it promptly in this chamber, but not to make an elaborate speech dealing with his relation as a business man and merchant and lumber man with the government of the province of Quebec or any other province. The distinction is clear. It is mentioned in the books with great particularity.

I will pass on to the next move my hon. friend made, which was to quote from citation 161 set forth in the rules of the house. That citation had reference to the question of punishment for libel. I do not believe that that was a pertinent

Privilege-Mr. Lacroix
citation. If my hon. friend had quoted citation 157 instead of 161 he would have seen that the rules of the house are to the effect that interference with or reflections upon members have been resented as indignities to the house itself. When the hon. member who has raised the question of privilege has been reflected upon as one who is unworthy to sit in any house, surely that is an indignity to the House of Commons itself. In my opinion he should be allowed the fullest latitude to make clear his position with respect to all the circumstances that have occasioned the reflections which have been made.
May I add this, that the premier of Quebec stands in a very exceptional and very privileged position, and when, from his privileged and high position as premier of his province, he makes a charge against an hon. member of this house which cannot be replied to in the house in which it is made, surely that hon. member should be granted the fullest latitude to defend his honour and to make clear his position in relation to the situation referred to.

With respect to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh), and referred to by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) I hold that it is not well taken. Standing order No. 16 states clearly:
Whenever any matter of privilege arises, it shall be taken into consideration immediately.
I have listened to the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) and his explanation, and I think the facts he has stated justify him in rising in this house and stating his point of privilege. I would ask him to be as brief as possible, but he has a right to explain his point of privilege.

maintopic: PRESS REPORTS OP STATEMENTS MADE BEFORE THE PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE OF THE QUEBEC LEGISLATURE
speechtext:
If the prime minister of Quebec had really been prompted by that spirit of justice which must always be based on Christian charity, he would not have singled out the member for Beauce in connection with logging operations in Daaquam township, but would also have referred to previous and later companies whose policy has been similar to mine, unless his purpose was to show once more his gratitude to those powerful companies for which he has so much sympathy.
I may add that the Taschereau government never granted favours either to myself or to my companies, because I never requested any. Besides, I do believe that, under certain circumstances of which every one is aware, 51952-131
if I had been granted favours, they would have been made public.
The Hon. Mr. Duplessis endeavoured to show that I have shipped 40,000 logs from the Lac Portage district to the state of Maine, and this as long ago as 1924.
Here is my answer: never, absolutely never did I purchase from the Quebec government any timber in the Lac Portage district, and in order to show still further that Mr. Duplessis' statement was untrue, I have here, Mr. Speaker, the Contracts whereby I purchased 227,484-29 cords of wood at a cost of $828,922.02 from the company which enjoys Mr. Duplessis' friendship, that is John Breakey Limited. Under this contract, I was permitted by these same people, who are friends of Mr. Duplessis, to build a sluice, and to use the water of lake Portage for driving my logs into the state of Maine. Those same people, friends of Mr. Duplessis, had the government's authorization to sell me that timber. Such authorization was granted to them through another of Mr. Duplessis' friends, Mr. Thomas Maher, a forestry engineer and a former organizer for the Conservative party in the province of Quebec. And from the receipt which I found on Mr. Breakey's file at the time he transferred the title to me, I noticed that the other friend of Mr. Duplessis had received $10,000 from the Breakey Company for having secured that favour.
It will thus be seen, Mr. Speaker, that even under the former government, whose actions are now being scrutinized, the people who were receiving or requesting favours were not always those to whom Mr. Duplessis is referring, but rather people who were consorting with Mr. Duplessis.
Finally, Mr. Duplessis endeavoured to show that I had been desirous of securing an appointment as Minister of Lands and Forests, in Quebec. I am unafraid of any comparison between my ambitions and those of Mr. Duplessis but I am loath to discuss the subject. However, for the information of Mr. Duplessis, and in order to gratify wishes which are those of an inquisitor and a sadistic politician, I may tell him that in this respect he was again mistaken, because I might have been a minister, if such had been my wish, for the good reason that I was offered a portfolio.
Mr. Speaker, I may say in conclusion that I do protest, because my case is similar to that of a number of other Canadians from my own province, and because Mr. Duplessis, in order to hold his sway, is resorting in our province to the tactics used by a Stalin in Russia. Stalin kills, Duplessis debases.

subtopic: PROPOSED ABOLITION OF APPEALS TO HIS MAJESTY IN COUNCIL-CONSIDERATION OF BILL ON FRIDAY, APRIL 8
speechtext:
That the order for second reading of Bill No. 19, an act respecting appeals to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council be taken into consideration after routine proceedings on Friday next, the 8th instant, and that this order have precedence over all other business on that day.
He said: If the house will permit me I should like to amend the motion by dropping the concluding words

. . . and that this order have precedence over all other business on that day.
At the time I handed the notice to the clerk I assumed that as we were adjourning for the Easter vacation on Friday night it would in all probability be the wish of hon. members to have this particular bill occupy most of the time for discussion on Friday, and to have this known in advance. However, at the time I thought that greater progress would have been made with certain private and other bills in the interval. I see that on Tuesday night last the bill in respect to the Niagara Falls Observation Bridge Company in particular was again talked out. As the opportunities to discuss these measures are few we ought not I think to take away an opportunity on Friday night of this week. I might say in regard to the Niagara Falls Observation Bridge Bill that the government is wholly favourable to the enactment of the measure, and I think all hon. members on this side are in sympathy with it. At any rate if the motion in its present form were to stand I am afraid the impression might be created that it has been framed with a view of precluding discussion on Friday night of the measure I have mentioned. So I should like to have the motion amended in that particular.
In regard to the motion itself may I say that the government feels that the bill in the name of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) in respect of appeals to the privy council deals with a question of great interest, particularly at this time when constitutional questions are much to the fore. We believe it would be in every way in the public interest to have the measure fully discussed on at least one day during the session. Some little time ago the government gave the hon. member to understand that if he would not press his bill at the time, an opportunity would be given later for him to bring it before the house. I hope therefore that hon. members will see their way to adopt the motion.
Motion as amended agreed to.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, April 5, consideration in committee of the following proposed resolution-Mr. Rogers

Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide assistance towards the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress, and for such payments out of moneys appropriated by parliament as may be necessary for all or any of the purposes of the proposed legislation.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the sole purpose of my few and rather brief remarks is to direct the attention of the government to the increase in relief and unemployment that is taking place in this country and that has taken place during the last few months. Naturally I should like to find out what the government is going to do in order to deal with this condition. Last Monday afternoon and evening I listened carefully, and I may say hopefully, to the long address of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) introducing the resolution providing for grants in order to alleviate agricultural and economic distress. I say I listened hopefully, because .1 expected that the minister was going to suggest some scheme or plan to cope with our present unemployment problem, which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said was Canada's most urgent national problem'. However, I was greatly disappointed. The minister reviewed briefly the report of the national employment commission and dealt rather vaguely with the potential value oft the tourist trade. He finished up by eulogizing the trade policies of the government, which he claimed had brought prosperity to this country.
The minister did not seem to be aware that during the past few months the industries of this country have been slowing down because of the importations of foreign manufactured
goods which have been flooding our market. Hamilton, being a large industrial centre, has suffered more keenly than many other centres. It has felt the effects of the recession to a considerable extent and the increased burden of relief is becoming so great that the government no longer can evade the responsibility of assuming the maintenance of our unemployed. In December, 1937, there were 2,607 heads of families on relief in Hamilton. In January, 1938, the number had increased to 2,982. In that month there were 9,120 dependants and 684 individuals on relief, a total of 12,863 persons. In February the number of heads of families on relief had increased to 3,247; the dependants had increased to 10,050 and the individuals to 740, making a grand total of 14,037. I have not the exact figures for March, but I am informed that there is a considerable increase.
There are also hundreds and hundreds of men who are working two, three and four days per week. These men are merely existing, and unless conditions improve, in a short time they too will be on relief. There are also many men possessing abundant health and ability who are unable to obtain employment because of their age. Men of thirty-eight, forty-two and forty-five years of age find it exceedingly difficult to secure employment. Their condition is as bad as, if not worse than, that of the western farmer, who at least can hope for a crop some time in the future.
Foreign manufactured goods are being sold in this country at ridiculously low prices, prices with which our Canadian manufacturers cannot possibly compete. I was advised last week in Hamilton that shoes are being imported from a foreign country at a cost of eighty cents per pair. It would cost our manufacturers at least $2.50 to produce a similar pair of shoes. Dresses are being sold at $1.25; our Canadian manufacturers would have to charge $6 or $8 for a similar product. I could give innumerable examples of subsidized foreign goods and goods made with cheap labour being dumped on our home markets. This decreases the market of the Canadian manufacturer and adds to our unemployment. I attribute these conditions to the government's trade policies which have not adequately protected the home market in order that our Canadian manufacturers might obtain a fair share.
I have one other observation to make. It has been the policy of governments in depression times in the past to attempt to stimulate the construction industry by spend-
20S4

Relief and Agricultural Distress
ing millions of dollars on public works, many of which were not actually needed. While these methods have met with some success, I do not think they are practicable to-day. This government has attempted to stimulate the construction industry by making available cheap and easy money, but it has met with only partial success. The reason for its failure is the fact that the bulk of our construction work is carried on in the municipalities. Because of debt charges and the increasing cost of social services, particularly unemployment relief, our municipalities are compelled to impose such heavy taxes on real property that it is no longer desirable or profitable to build, buy or even hold such property. As in the case of the automobile, it is not the initial cost but the upkeep that is so heavy. I urge strongly that the government assume the burden of maintaining our unemployed, making sure that the benefits of this policy are conferred on the property owner. If this were done I believe much good would result, not only to the municipalities but also to the government.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) will readily admit that when he introduced his motion on Monday last hon. members gave him an attentive hearing. The people of this country were looking forward with a good deal of eagerness to what the minister would have to say. As a member of this house I awaited the minister's statement in the hope that he would divulge the plans of the government to meet the pressing problem of unemployment and relief. We expected him not only to tell us something about the relief problem, but to go fully into the policy that the government had in mind to meet the situation that now confronts us.
My own eager anticipation of that occasion was manifested by the simple fact of my taking a few sheets of note paper out of my desk and placing them before me, with the idea of jotting down from time to time anything of interest and importance. Like many other hon. members, within the next few days I shall be going back to my constituency. In my constituency, as in those of many other hon. members, there are many men and women who are in want, who are unemployed or on the verge of being unemployed. I was anxious to take back to my constituents and to others whom I would meet in other parts of the dominion some ray of hope, something in the way of a policy which the government had to meet the existing situation. So, Mr. Chairman, I placed these few sheets of paper before me, and I waited for half an hour in the hope that I 
could jot something down, but there was nothing to record. The hour went by and I still had nothing to write down. Two hours went by, and the sheets in front of me were still blank. Three hours went by, and still they were blank. Just after the third hour had gone by the minister sat down, and I was still looking at those sheets of paper in front of me and wondering what I could tell the people of the city of Winnipeg.
The minister did say something that was of interest and possibly of importance so far as the administration of relief is concerned. But relief is only part of the problem of unemployment, and I was not so anxious to hear the minister deal with relief as I was to hear him deal with the fundamental question of the unemployed in this dominion; and on that question the minister had very little to say, I will say this, however, that the few remarks he did make on that question did not give the unemployed very much hope for the immediate future.
The minister dealt, for instance, with the drought situation. He said that the conditions in the industrial centres in western Canada were reflecting agricultural conditions in that part of the country. There may be a certain amount of truth in that, but I do not think the minister, who is such a close student of economics, would agree or that he would teach a body of students of economics that the unemployment and the poverty existing in western Canada are due to the fact that western Canada has had poor crops for the last two or three years. If he would, then, speaking in an economic sense, what would the minister have to say as to the unemployment situation that developed between the years 1929 and 1933, when similar conditions prevailed in our industrial centres in the "west, not because we had a drought in the west but because we had too much of everything at that time.
So the position is that we have poverty when we have too much of everything; and, if we happen to have a lack of moisture in western Canada, then we blame unemployment and poverty on the lack of moisture.
I do wish that the minister when he deals with this problem as it affects the people of western Canada in particular would go a little deeper into the fundamental aspects of the question instead of dealing with it in a more or less superficial way.
The minister had two suggestions to make, two items, shall I say, which may be regarded as constituting the policy of the government in coping with the situation. One was the tourist traffic, and the other the Canada-United States trade agreement looking towards an expansion of our trade with the

Relief and Agricultural Distress
country to the south of us. In regard to foreign trade, if the minister and the government are going to take credit for the improved economic conditions that existed in this country during the past two years up until last fall, whose is the responsibility for the conditions that have prevailed since? If the Canada-United States trade agreement was responsible for the improvement in trade up until a few months ago, what is responsible for the recession that has set in during . the past few months? I am one of those who voted for the Canada-United States trade agreement. I am in favour of liberating trade wherever we possibly can; I am in favour of reducing tariffs wherever we possibly can, but side by side with that statement I say that in the reduction of tariffs there is not to be found the solution for the economic conditions that prevail in the Dominion of Canada. And may I say to my friends to my right, in exactly the same way, that in increasing tariffs there is not to be found any solution for our economic conditions. because if an increase in tariffs would have brought about a solution of our problems they would have been solved immediately after the year 1930-31.
May I say a word in regard to the importance of the unemployment situation? Its importance is not to be measured merely by the numbers who are unemployed at the present time, or by the numbers who are working short time. Its importance must be measured also by the uncertainty which prevails amongst hundreds of thousands of men who are to-day engaged in industry but do not know how long their jobs are going to last. It is that very uncertainty that is one of the worst features of the whole of our unemployment problem. For these men unemployed or partially employed, to tramp the streets to look for that elusive job which they know in fact does not exist is one of the hardest tasks which men and women have to face. The average worker who is employed to-day is not very far removed from poverty. Two or three weeks' or a month's unemployment puts him in the poverty line, where soon he will be compelled, generally against his own wishes, to become the recipient of public or private charity.
I should like the minister to have given us a more realistic viewpoint of the existing economic conditions in this dominion. He told us of the expansion of trade during the past two years. I. think we will all admit there has been improvement in that respect, and we were all in a way pleased to note the expansion of industry, but I should like to have had a concrete view, if possible, of the
extent to which that expansion was due to preparations for war either in this dominion or in other parts of the world.
May I point out that the industries of this country are to a certain extent dependent upon what is taking place in other parts of the world, and not so much upon tariffs?
The minister spoke of the tourist traffic and hoped for its expansion. With improved economic conditions in the United States we have had an expansion of tourist traffic. The better the economic conditions in the United States were, the more tourists came to Canada. But if there is a recession in industry in the United States, you will find a decrease in the tourist traffic in Canada from the United States, which sends us more tourists than any other nation in the world. Anything the government might do to increase the tourist traffic would be of little value unless you have improved economic conditions in other parts of the world. Whilst I am on that aspect of the question, may I add further that we in this country are the beneficiaries to a very large extent of the expenditure of many hundreds of millions of dollars by the Roosevelt administration in an attempt to bring about better economic conditions in the United States. Money spent in the United States in some measure finds its way here through the purchase of our lumber, for instance, to improve the housing conditions in the United States, and through an increased purchase of our paper and other supplies. But a recession in industry in the United States was followed at once by a falling off in the demand from the United States for our lumber and our paper and other products. Of course, the government of this country, no matter what its political complexion may be, could take no credit for the vast spending that has been done in the United States under the Roosevelt administration.
I wish to make a few remarks in connection with the national employment commission, which has just about passed out of existence. That commission was ushered into existence with a great flourish of trumpets, but hardly a word was said when it passed out. For years we were told what it was going to do; great expectations were held out to the people as to what would happen when this commission was appointed. As far back as 1933, speaking in this chamber, the present Prime Minister, outlining the policy of the Liberal party, said:
The Liberal party believes unemployment is Canada's most urgent national problem. It would deal with the present emergency conditions through a representative national commission, which would cooperate with the
Relief and Agricultural Distress

provinces and municipalities in the administration of unemployment relief and in an endeavour to provide work for the unemployed.
Is there any hon. member who would say that, such a commission having been appointed, its work is now finished? Why was the commission put out of existence? I am beginning to wonder whether it was ever wanted by the Department of Labour, because if it really was wanted and became an integral part of activities directed to providing employment, it would after having been in existence about eighteen months perform its most useful functions. But after an existence of about a year and a half it is put out of business by a stroke of a pen.

The fact is that they were never asked to be a part of an administrative body. That is admitted in their own report. They were not even asked to become a supervisory body, but just a consultative body, to tell the government that certain things were desirable; that they may do only certain things, but when it comes to the question of performing real tasks their services are no longer required.

Now, to go back to speeches made in this house in the year 1936, let me quote what the present Prime Minister stated on that very question:
The people of Canada will never know the cost of relief until there is some agency to bring together in one report the expenditures of all the agencies involved, government and private alike, nor will there be any substantial lessening in the amounts until they know the manner in which all the different agencies are supervising their expenditures and carrying out the works for which the expenditures are being made. That is one of the main purposes of this commission, and I venture to say that no agency other than a body such as we suggest can possibly carry it out.
Speaking on the same occasion, the Prime Minister made several references along the same line. I quote this one:
If a matter affecting municipal, provincial and dominion funds is to be dealt with satisfactorily, it is essential that the party who deals with it be above all, but not part of, any one of these particular entities. That is why we need a commission of this kind to assist in the distribution of outlays and in the supervision of expenditures.
I shall quote one other statement of the Prime Minister on the same day:
It is not to take responsibility away from any department of the government. The work to be done will be carried out under the several government departments, but there will be one body which shall have the power to supervise all the work and to see that it is properly correlated in affording the employment anticipated ; also to advise the government with respect to what may be desirable courses to pursue. Not only that, the commission will have power to take a similar birdseye view with respect to what is being done to provide employment and relief in each and all of the provinces, what is being done in the municipalities, and what is and may be done by private industry.	-
None of these functions has been performed by this commission. I do not know why. Probably the minister knows better than any other hon. member. My own viewpoint is that he decided that the commission was an unnecessary adjunct of the Department of Labour, and possibly his department may be able to perform the functions that were being performed by the commission. But my main point is that for a period of two to three years the people of this country were led to believe that, with the appointment of a commission to deal with unemployment, we would have a body that would do something worth while to cope fundamentally with that problem, and no sooner had it been appointed and the members had, so to speak, warmed their seats, than they were told that their services were no longer required.

I come to some of the recommendations of the commission-which were unanimous- and the attitude of the minister thereto.
The first was the need for early action to provide low-rental housing. If I understood the implications of the speech that the Minister of Labour made in this chamber on Monday last, we are not going to have very much low rental housing at this session of parliament-

I need hardly say that in the last election and prior thereto the people of this country were given definite promises that during this parliament the government would undertake large schemes of low rental housing and schemes of slum clearances. I believe they were told that over the radio just on the eve of the election. I should like to know why those promises were made and nothing done to fulfil them. regard to human needs, to the furtherance of social justice, and to the promotion of the common good."

Let me finish the statement:
I believe the country would welcome, above all else, a comprehensive scheme of urban and rural improvements. Such a scheme would appropriately include the clearance of slum areas, housing programs, the painting and repair of buildings and fences, both in the cities and the country; and, of scenic development, which would serve to make of Canada a country second to none for tourists, and to afford to the people as a whole fuller opportunities of recreation and the enjoyment of natural beauty.
I am asked from what I was quoting. I was just quoting from speeches made by the Prime Minister in 1935.
I come now to the other recommendations of the commission, the second being the creation of a national tourist committee. I do not think the unemployed will get very much consolation from that. The others deal more or less with agricultural rehabilitation and other methods of dealing with the question of relief. As I said before, relief is only a part of the problem of unemployment and I would rather have it done away with entirely. What I should like to see is provision whereby the people of the country might earn their own livelihood. Instead of devoting four-fifths of his speech to details of administration with regard to relief, however important that may be from the administrative standpoint, I think it would have been better had the minister given us some idea of the government's program for dealing with the existing situation. Since the minister made his speech it has been announced that the government is going to spend large sums of money for the purpose of providing employment. I have no objection to expenditures for this purpose, but I believe the minister will agree with me that no form of capital expenditure can be a cure for the problem of unemployment. In my humble opinion the piling up of a debt burden will only aggravate an already serious situation. If we are to tackle this important problem of unemployment we must deal with it in a more fundamental way than by merely expending large sums of public money which only add to the national debt burden.
So far we have had no indication of the government's policy apart from the expanding of foreign trade. We find that to-day there is a contraction in our foreign markets and we
20S8
Relief and Agricultural Distress

begin to realize at once how little we can depend on those markets as a means of enabling us to cope with our internal problems.

speechtext: My hon. friend, I know, is keenly interested in this question. He says that what we should look for is employment and I agree with him absolutely. He has considered the possibilities of increasing employment, but he does not believe that there is any hope in an expansion of trade, nor does he believe that it is a wise policy to make capital expenditures for the purpose of providing employment. I agree with him that expenditures of that kind, if they are to be justified, must lead ultimately to an increase in national income. That is their essential justification. But I do not think that he has thrown any light on the situation. He has said that you cannot provide sufficient employment through expanding trade. He has said that you cannot provide employment usefully by means of large capital expenditures. He has also said that we ought not to continue relief. What does he suggest?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I did not say that we ought not to do those things; I said that they are not a solution.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: What is the solution, then?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I say that capital expenditures are not a solution for the unemployment problem.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Nor is expansion of trade, according to the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The granting of relief is not a solution. The mere fact of obtaining wider markets for our products is not in my opinion a solution, and I think that is evident: throughout this period of seven or eight years we have been faced with acute unemployment. What can we do? I am in favour of a comprehensive housing scheme, a scheme of clearing away slums, to provide employment and at the same time give to the people of the country proper housing accommodation; and I believe in doing this through the^ public treasury without adding to the national debt. That is the difference between the hon. gentleman and myself. I do not believe that the government are prepared to do that. I would also provide for public works along the same line. In 1934 the previous government provided approximately $34,000,000 for public works through the creation of additional currency and nothing serious happened.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is incorrect as to the amount.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

I understand that S35,000,000 was printed and a part of it was used for a public works program. The money was printed as part of the government's policy and no harm came to the country. I suggest that we could enter upon a comprehensive housing scheme, with all our natural resources, without having to borrow from private interests. Personally I cannot see anything wrong about a principle of that kind, but the government will not accept it.
I would go a little further. The moment we suggest that the needs of our people should be satisfied first, before we look to the export of commodities, we are told that we are economic nationalists. What I am trying to do is to bring about economic sanity in the affairs of the country. The minister told us on Monday that from certain parts of Canada we were exporting to other parts of the world, halibut, salmon and apples. What consolation is it to the million people on relief to-day to tell them that we are sending out of Canada the foodstuffs that they should be given the first opportunity of consuming? Under a proper system of planned economy it would be possible to distribute those commodities among our own people. Our own Canadian people who in their general capacity have helped to produce that wealth should have the first claim upon it. That is where we differ from the government. They would rather export these goods to people in other parts of the world than see our own people consume them. I would prefer to see our own Canadian people given the first opportunity to acquire the goods produced in the dominion.
I wish now to deal with one or two other questions touched upon by the Minister of Labour in relation to matters contained in the report. We w'ere led to believe, prior to the election, that we might have a scheme of unemployment insurance in Canada, and amongst those who believe they would become beneficiaries of such a scheme there are many who think that all the unemployed would automatically come within its purview. The commission, I believe, has correctly pointed out that the experience of other countries shows that no unemployment insurance system can carry the full burden of unemployment. Provision must be made for those who cannot qualify for unemployment insurance, and for workers who exhaust their benefits under such a plan through prolonged idleness. I am becoming more and more convinced as time goes on, especially with the recurring periods of unemployment coming in much shorter cycles than twenty or thirty

Relief and Agricultural Distress
years ago, that any unemployment insurance scheme introduced under existing economic conditions can reach no more than an extremely small proportion of unemployed men. Those whom an unemployment insurance * scheme is likely to include are those in more or less permanent employment, the ones least likely to need the benefits. Consequently the hope that vast numbers of workers may have had of benefiting by an unemployment insurance scheme are not as great as it may have been in years gone by.
I remember when an unemployment insurance scheme was first introduced in the British house, about thirty years ago. At that time the government and those engaged in the statistical survey of unemployment could measure the amount of unemployment with reasonable accuracy. They could say that it would vary in a given period of years from five to ten per cent. But to-day the variation is ever so much greater. I think
160.000	was the number given by the minister the other day.

In fact from the time the interim report was made public until to-day, when the final report of the commission is before us-in just those few months-there has been a vast change in the economic situation in this country. If such a change can take place in a few months, what is likely to happen in two or three years? The cycles recur more frequently and their magnitude is greater than in the past. Instead of a variation of five to ten per cent it may be as high as thirty per cent, and no unemployment insurance scheme that the government can introduce could ever take care of such numbers of unemployed as we have had in years gone by.
One thing I did hope the commission might recommend was something in the way of relief for our municipalities. But they have not touched that feature at all. In fact they suggest that we proceed on almost the same lines as before in dealing with this problem.
And evidently that is about the policy which the government itself is adopting. I should like, however, to quote a few words spoken by the Minister of Labour in this house on March 30, 1936, because they are quite applicable to what we are discussing now. He said, as reported on page 1569 of Hansard:
The problem of prolonged unemployment in this and other countries is a challenge to the political intelligence of our generation.
With that statement I am in full accord. Then he went on to say:
As individuals we must guard ourselves against the complacent acceptance of conditions as we find them to-day. As members of parliament and as a government the placid acceptance of present conditions would be little better than a voluntary declaration of political bankruptcy.
But it seems to me that the government is now accepting conditions as they are. I could quote a number of other statements which the Minister of Labour made on that occasion. I have no doubt that when he spoke in this chamber on March 30, 1936, he did so with a sense of the onerous responsibilities devolving upon him and with the intention of doing all that was best under the circumstances, no doubt he thought he would be able to put into effect policies which would bring about the improved conditions which I am sure he desired then, and desires now. He said significantly that if he could not do that it was a challenge to our intelligence and an indication of political bankruptcy.
I wish now to deal briefly with the aspect of the question to which I referred to a moment ago, that of the burden of unemployment relief on the municipalities. We are bound to admit that the municipalities are not responsible for the condition of unemployment in Canada to-day. It is most unfair on the part of the national government and this house that the greater part of the burden arising from this condition should fall upon our municipal authorities. I do not know whether the minister was so sure in his own mind about the statement he made the other day as to the burden upon our municipalities. He said that in certain municipalities the standard of relief was such that it competed with the labour market in that area, the implication being that the standard of relief in those areas was too high. In fairness to the municipalities which may be implicated, and in order that they may refute the statement if they can, I should like the minister to say which municipalities were giving too high a scale of relief. I am wondering whether the minister had in mind the city of Winnipeg. I have heard it said that Winnipeg is



Relief and Agricultural Distress
giving the unemployed too much. I had sent to me recently a statement of the scale of relief which the municipal authorities of Winnipeg are giving to the recipients of public relief; here it is. A family of two persons, husband and wife, for unemployment relief food allowance and other sundries in the home, such as soap, etc., receives for a month the equivalent of S12.76. Three dollars a week for two persons to live on in Winnipeg! Is there any hon. member here who will say that is too high? Yet we are told that in some municipalities the standard of relief is too 'high. So the scale goes on until the highest is reached-$41.64 per month for food for a family of two grown-ups and six dependent children, in other words a little less than $10 a week for food for eight persons! I do not think a little over $1125 per week per person in a family of eight could by the greatest stretch of the imagination be said to be too much. I think in fairness to the municipalities he had in mind the minister should state which cities were giving too much by way of relief, and give them an opportunity to state their side of the question.
There is also the question of the financial burden on the municipalities. In 1929 the city of Winnipeg spent $25,914 in the way of unemployment relief, and I think in a comparative sense the figures I am giving would be applicable to almost any large industrial area in Canada. The year 1929 was during the period which we commonly term the highest peak of prosperity in this country, although I must admit that it was only a onesided prosperity. In 1937, however, for its share of unemployment relief the city of Winnipeg had to spend the sum of $1,530,015. That is the extent to which it had grown. Over a period of seven years, from 1931 to 1937 inclusive, the city of Winnipeg had to spend approximately $10,000,000 in the way of public relief. How can any municipality stand such heavy expenditures? Winnipeg cannot. In 1929 and 1930 Winnipeg was one of the best financed cities in Canada. It had a sinking fund equal to the best to be found anywhere on the north American continent; but to-day, as the result of capital expenditures involved in connection with unemployment relief over a period of more than seven years, the banks refuse to grant the city further credit. That S10,000,000 means that out of revenue the city of Winnipeg must make an annual expenditure of $550,000 for interest charges.
I think in considering this whole question of relief the government ought to come to the aid of our municipalities and relieve them of

this burden, in order that they may fulfil the functions they ought to fulfil as municipal bodies. Under present circumstances it is almost impossible for Winnipeg, together with a great many other cities in the west and probably in the east as well, to carry on. They find themselves on the verge of bankruptcy, due to this load of unemployment relief for which they are in no way responsible. I would plead with the minister that the government make additional grants in aid to the provinces so that this aid may be passed on to the municipalities, thereby recognizing the responsibility of the federal government for the unemployment situation in Canada. That it is recognized as a federal responsibility is shown by the fact that to-day we are told that the government will expend large sums of money for public works.
When these expenditures are being considered by the government I believe they should be made in municipalities where they are most needed. I do not care whether the municipalities are in the east or the west; I should like to see the government give most where the need is greatest.

Further, I should like to congratulate him upon his lucid speech, but as I read it I was reminded of the language of Winston Churchill, who, in speaking of another, said in essence that his own native lucidity of expression was a great handicap to him when he had so little to say.
The speech of the minister deals with a problem that goes to the very depths of our national life and is, as the minister himself states, without question the most vital and pressing of all the problems with which we have to deal. The minister spoke for a space of three hours, during which he purported to cover the whole broad problem. He dealt

with many different points, but perhaps if he should ask himself what the man on relief feels to-day as a result of what the minister said in his three hour speech, he might well ponder upon the reply. Does the man on relief to-day feel encouraged as a result of the minister's speech? There are in this dominion at this very moment hundreds of thousands who are dependent upon the payment of relief and who look to the bounty of the government for mere sustenance. They are as well looking to the government to take some action to improve the lot in which they find themselves to-day due to no fault of their own. Is there any member of this committee who feels for a moment that those on relief to-day, those who are employable but unemployed or those who are employed for part time, can take encouragement out of anything that has been said by the minister? I have under my hand the "final" report dated January 26, 1938, of the national employment commission. Within the covers of this report there is much to which all hon. rpembers may subscribe. Unquestionably the commission has done its job honestly and well within the limits of its ability, but what is to be the fate of its final report? What is to be done with these recommendations? The house has witnessed during the last session or two what has happened to many reports. There have been interim reports of this commission, and what treatment have they received? I shall return to that in a few moments, but now we are told by the minister that the findings of the commission are to be held pending the report of the Rowell commission. One commission reports to another. It sounds very much like a double play in a baseball game, "Rogers to Purvis to Rowell." Here we have one commission set up to accomplish a definite purpose and to make recommendations to the government. Those recommendations are made, and now we are told that we must wait. The commission was fully conscious of its own position in this matter, for if we turn to page 8 of their report we find this language, referring to the work done by the employment commission:
The extensive work done during the last twelve months will undoubtedly be of considerable value to the new commission.
This is an expression of opinion from the national employment commission, in its own report, referring to the new commission which is to follow it. After all, we in Canada today find ourselves faced with the well known

Liberal policy of another year and another country, a "wait and see" policy strangely reminiscent to those who read history of the policies adopted by Lord Asquith by which he paved the way for the disintegration of the British Liberal policy. Wait and see! Well, Mr. Chairman, I think we have to admit that the government has great "weight" of numbers, but it seems to be completely at "sea" in this matter.
What great work has been done; what great accomplishment has been achieved by the government in connection with the matter before us at the present time? The national expenditure for the whole of Canada in 1930-31 amounted to $4,750,000,000. Of this amount 3-5 per cent, or S165,250.000, was spent for our educational institutions, our schools and universities. On the same basis as that which I have just stated, that is, if we were to spend 3'5 per cent only of our national income for the purpose of training youth-and by national income I mean income for which this government is responsible-we would spend 3-5 per cent of $450,000,000, or $15,750,000, for the training of our youth. And yet we grant only one-sixteenth of that amount.
Hon. members will recall what was commenced under the Technical Education Act of 1919. Here a sum of money was granted

to the various provinces, a grant in aid for the purpose of stimulating-I believe that is the correct word-technical education. The results have been most, satisfactory as far as they have gone. In 1921, as a direct result of these government grants, technical education received a rare stimulus, so that ten years later we find that 121,000 young people were enrolled in our technical schools. Here it seems to me is categorical proof of the efficiency of direct grants in aid to the provinces for the purpose of education. At that time the bugaboo of interference with the provinces, of the usurpation of provincial rights by the federal government, was overcome without any difficulty whatsoever. The provinces accepted these grants and put them to a useful purpose, and they were glad to get them, with the result that technical education in this country received a stimulus which has been a great blessing to those who took advantage of it.
Let us compare the present situation with the past. Here we are to-day facing a national situation created by what has been called the depression, and which to-day is referred to as the recession, when tens of thousands of our young people are failing to get not only technical education but education of all sorts beyond a certain point. Surely the situation is far worse than it was in 1919-1920 immediately after the war. Surely the minister realizes himself that what was done then was a success, and that what can be done now could also be a success. But here we are*granting only $1,000,000, and I protested in this chamber last session with all the vehemence of which I was capable against the small amount of this grant. The principle of it is sound. I am not criticizing any one of the courses set up as far as they go, but I do complain of the extent of the grant. When we were dealing with an emergency in the two western provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, we poured out of the treasury of this dominion, $22,390,000 under governor general's warrants because there was an emergency. I am not minimizing for a moment the desirability of sending that money to Saskatchewan and Alberta where it will be put to the most useful of purposes, the maintenance of life and of those things which maintain life. Here is an emergency situation; we sent $22,390,000 to the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan because we have to do so. That $22,390,000 is to cure nothing except an immediate situation; it is to cure no cancprous ill but is merely to meet an emergen; y. It is man's answer to an act of God.

It seems to me that here is an example of what we are doing in so many different ways in this dominion. We are temporizing with the results of situations which we have failed to face. We are not getting down to and dealing with fundamental causes. If we were to spend such an amount as we have sent out to Alberta and Saskatchewan, because we had to do so, on education and leamership courses or apprenticeships-call it what you want- no one can estimate what the results would be in this dominion for the possible returns are immeasurable.
Some of us have had an opportunity of visiting Sweden and Denmark in recent years, and one realizes that their young men and young women who have shown ability to assimilate education are provided with an opportunity to develop themselves into useful productive citizens by having made available to them to the fullest possible extent the country's educational system. The hon. member for Essex East last session introduced most ably a resolution in regard to scholarships. What has happened? We have our 81,000,000, but how far does it go? We must realize that when we spend $1,000,000 on youth reestablishment in this country, we are spending only one-fifth of one per cent of our national income and devoting only that relatively petty and puny amount to youth reestablishment. What shortsightedness is here!
Within the report there is much with which I agree. But on page 12 I read this paragraph :
In view of its importance, the commission has, in recent months, discussed this problem with all provincial governments, and has also taken active steps to educate public opinion as to the necessity for action so as to provide the appropriate background for practical achievement.
With all respect for the commission, that is the remark of an adolescent. "To educate public opinion," in connection with that with which we are dealing! Surely it is obvious on every hand that public opinion is stirred almost to the breaking point, because the government are taking no direct, forward steps to deal with this question with which they perforce must deal. They are temporizing with the situation and not dealing with its fundamental cause. Educate public opinion!' I should think the government would hope that public opinion would not be stirred up any further than it is at the present moment. "Wait and see."
Let us return to the minister's remarks of last Monday. As reported at page 1995 of Hansard, he said:
For that reason I want to say frankly to the committee that we as a government did not feel it was desirable, at this stage at any rate, that we should by dominion legislation seek to invade the field of apprenticeship. There have been cases before-and they have been brought to the attention of the house-where the dominion government has by a grant in aid induced provinces-at least they have occasionally told us afterwards that they were induced -more or less, the assumption has been, against their will, into new directions of expenditure. I need only mention agricultural instruction and technical education. Once we have gone into those fields the tendency has always been to make what was designed as a temporary expenditure into a permanent expenditure, and in this way to bring about as it were a transfer of provincial obligations to the dominion by a back-door route, and that has not been a satisfactory method of dealing with the situation.
And then later:
Particularly at the present time, I do not think it is advisable that the dominion government should assume what might be regarded as legislative jurisdiction. . . .
Those are the minister's comments with regard to apprenticeship. Does he really feel that an effort to reintroduce the apprenticeship system into the Dominion of Canada means that we are invading the provinces by the back door? Having the high regard I have for the minister, and the high respect I have for his native intelligence, I cannot but feel that he knows in his own heart that it would not be a back-door practice. It might appear such to some if they wished to misconstrue it, but the minister knows and I know that it is not a back-door method to do what was done in 1919 under the Technical Education Act. The minister knows full well that if it had not been for that act and the putting of it into practice as was done, technical education in this dominion would not be one-half as far along the way as it is.

3.	Qualifications for selection.
4.	Fixed period for apprenticeship courses.
5.	For apprenticeship only, a written indenture between apprentice, his parent or guardian and employer.
6.	Compulsory government registration and supervision of all approved apprenticeship and learnership plans.
7.	Maintenance of craft standards by definite schedules and standards of training-with periodic tests and granting of official diplomas.
8.	Fixed period for class instruction of all apprentices and obligatory attendance thereat.
9.	In the case of apprenticeship definite ratio of apprentices to journeymen.
10.	Progressive wage scale to provide apprentice with regular income.
11.	Plans to interlock with provincial vocational education.
12.	Establishment of advisory committees under provincial supervision for each trade, where feasible, to work out methods most suitable for the application of plans in designated areas or for particular industries.
13.	Appointment of vocational officers to cooperate with technical and secondary schools.
14.	Employer and employee organizations to be given every facility to become familiar with the work of technical schools and with the employment service; permission to be granted by industries to senior students and teachers. to visit and become acquainted with factory operations as far as may be practical.
15.	Revision of school curricula from time to time to bring same into harmony with the practical requirements of industry.
16.	Provision to be made in minimum wage laws for exemption of accredited apprentices where their wages are regulated by approved apprenticeship schemes.
That is the report on apprenticeship, by the national employment commission. The hon. member for Melfort can see that there are many different points connected with this matter. I fully admit that it is a complicated problem. But the question I want to ask the minister is: Have any attempts been made to make agreements with industry in regard to apprenticeship? What steps have been taken in cooperation with industry to reestablish what has been done in this regard? The minister in his speech did not make any reference to these matters, and I wondered, as I read the recommendations of the national employment commission-

speechtext:
What we have done, as my hon. friend is aware, is to enter into agreements with the provinces, and those agreements have contained schedules covering various training projects that involved occupational training which, in turn, involved cooperation with industry. But the administration of them has been with the provincial

governments concerned, even as the whole question of apprenticeship has been under the provincial governments, and I do not think anything could emphasize that more strongly than the various references in the report itself as contained on pages 40 and 41.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Yes. I have read it.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: A desirable thing is, it is suggested in the report, to link it up with technical and vocational training, which is provincial, and so on.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The question I had in mind was this. Perhaps there are two steps in the approach to the problem. First, there is the question of determining that provinces are willing to accept a grant in aid for such a reform; then, is the industry willing to cooperate with a provincial or any government as far as an apprenticeship system is concerned? Have any steps been taken to ascertain the latter rather than the former point?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I should say, both. But our contact as a federal government has been with the provinces. The provinces, in turn, have dealt with industry within provincial borders. There has been in some cases excellent cooperation on the part of industry. In other cases-I do not think I should make any invidious comparisons at this time-the cooperation has not been all that could have been desired.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The minister referred to the matter in these words:
I do not think it is advisable that the dominion parliament should assume what might be regarded as legislative jurisdiction over apprenticeship.
Does he regard these courses already set up as involving legislative jurisdiction?

speechtext: No.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Then we are comparing incomparables; the two are different. I could find in the minister's speech, or in the report no reference to the fact that industry had been consulted to see whether they were willing or not to cooperate in any governmental plan.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The provincial authorities, in carrying out the terms of the agreement, have been in consultation with industry.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: But there is no mention of agreement or otherwise here. The minister refers to no such agreement.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Agreements have been made between the Department of Labour and similar departments in all the provinces covering the training projects.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Let me repeat what the minister said:
I do not think it is advisable that the domitdon parliament should assume what might be regarded as legislative jurisdiction over apprenticeship.
Who wants legislative jurisdiction?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: A question was put to me by a member of the house, or there was criticism on the part of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Let me read the context:
Mr. Woodsworth: But surely if it is possible to do that in what are termed learnership courses, it would be possible to do it in the case of apprenticeship.
Mr. Rogers:	I shall not quarrel with my
hon. friend over the use of terms. But I shall say this, that, particularly at th* present time, I do not think it is advisable. . . .
My whole point is that it is not a question of legislative jurisdiction, but a question of cooperation, a question of working with industry-not working for industry, but working with industry. I repeat, I cannot find in the minister's speech nor can I find in the employment commission's report any reference that leads us to believe that industry has been consulted to see whether or not it is prepared to cooperate with any government, provincial or federal.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: As the minister has pointed out, the administration of this problem is in the hands of the provinces, and while some of the provinces have not cooperated to the extent we should like, some have. In Ontario, in my hon. friend's own city as well as in Windsor, men have been appointed and at this moment are making a canvass of industry in the community to ascertain the extent to which industry is prepared to cooperate with the government in this problem.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: It is hard to say to what matter the premier of Ontario refers at any time. The hon. member for Essex East will, however, agree with me in this. We were told in the election of 1935 that there would be great harmony between the federal government and each of at least eight of the nine provinces, were a Liberal government elected. There was even a love-feast in Toronto prior to the election. But now harmony is conspicuous by its absence, which seems to be highly regrettable. It is extremely unfortunate that as we rise in our places here to make a few remarks in regard to such a matter, we have to conjecture whether there will be harmony or not. The minister himself admits that the whole matter hinges on such harmony. It was successful in previous years because the provinces cooperated. I have here a list of what was spent in those years. But to-day youth is handicapped because two Liberal prime ministers cannot get along.

speechtext:
I do not think the Prime Minister will contradict that statement.
May I now refer as briefly as possible to the question of housing. At page 1990 of Hansard the minister is reported in regard to housing; he had a few remarks to make on the subject. Later on, after the dinner recess, at page 2000, he made a further reference. In the course of his speech, which fills no less than twenty-six pages of Hansard, he devoted only half a page to the important question of national housing. Why was so little said upon this subject? Because so little has been done. Let us look for a moment at the home improvement plan. The minister reports proudly that under the plan, which was itself under the aegis of the national employment commission, the sum of $15,000,000 has been spent in a year-splendid, as far as it goes. But I challenge the statement that the home improvement plan is some sort of serendipity, so that as a result of it some S60.000.000 or S70.000.000 have been spent in the building industry, that this sum has been spent as a result of the home improvement plan.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The hon. member for Davenport reminded me of that.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I cannot challenge so eminent an authority as either the minister or the hon. member for Davenport. I am, however, stating my own humble views, and I say that in my opinion the home improvement plan is not a serendipity. The minister as-

sumes that eighty-five per cent of what was spent under the home improvement plan was spent for labour, and that a $60,000,000 or $70,000,000 impetus was given to the building industry as a result of this plan, basing his figures on what was done in the United States. Well, let us see what has been done there compared with what we have achieved in Canada. The cities in the United States have done considerable work in slum clearance and home improvement. The housing division of the PWA has completed fifty-one projects, having expended $130 million. The minister probably knows of the Williamsburg homes in New York and other places. The housing division employed 102.000 men last year, and enabling acts were passed by various states without undue difficulty. Under the new United States housing act of 1937, twenty per cent of the cost of construction will be met by local and state government and twenty-five per cent by the federal government. And that was followed by the announcement on January 12, 193S, that S146.645.000 had been set aside for the use of forty cities-some $18,000,000 in New York, S4,900,000 in Buffalo, and so on. What have we done in Canada to stimulate building? Have we before us at this moment any low cost housing scheme? Has any such housing scheme been put forward to reduce unemployment? Definitely, yes. But the only direct action taken so far was taken under the Dominion Housing Act of 1935 before hon. gentlemen opposite came into office.
Let us turn for a moment to the final report of the national employment commission. At page 9 there appears this:
However, the revival of activity in house construction has not kept pace with the revival in other lines. Despite the shortage of housing in most parts of the country, people show little disposition to invest money in this field. There are several reasons for this attitude.
The commission goes on to list five reasons which it regards as adequate to explain the apathy of people in regard to the scheme. The commission feels very strongly on the subject, however, for at page 36 we find this language:
To direct expenditures on public works it is all-important that there should be added measures for stimulating private expenditures, of which successful examples are to be found in the Dominion Housing Act and the home improvement plan.
There are inherent difficulties in subsidizing employment in private industry, but the expenditure of public funds to promote private expenditures in providing more suitable housing for the country is desirable. In the field of slum clearance and the development of low

Reliej and Agricultural Distress
rental housing for those whose earning capacity does not enable them to live under conditions which are conducive to their own health and employability, or indeed to the public health, direct subsidizing of private and local initiative, whether by cash subsidy or by loan at less than commercial rates of interest, is desirable. This is only so, however, if adequate care is taken to ensure, first, that there is a supply of unemployed labour of the type required and, secondly, that the benefits of subsidization will go to the low income groups whose position it is desired to benefit.
Now, it is interesting to know on the basis of that thesis that the national employment commission were not derelict in their duty. They did submit a plan; it will be found on page 101 of their report, appendix E, "low rental housing plan." I shall not take the time of hon. members to read that plan, but it is worthy of being read with a great deal of care. There is much to warrant the exercise of critical judgment; there is much to commend this plan to our consideration. But when we turn to page 11 of the appendices we find this statement:
The plan recommended by the commission was put before the minister some time after the opening of the parliamentary session of 1937, and it is understood action thereon has been held over.
A plan was submitted. They even went so far as to submit a draft bill. The plan was submitted towards the beginning of the session of 1937. Here we are now in the middle or towards the end of the session of 1938, and we are still waiting to see. Why? Why has this plan not been brought forward? The minister gave his reason the other day, as reported on page 2000 of Hansard:
The national employment commission made proposals to the government last year with respect to low cost housing. These proposals were later given the form of a draft bill which reached the government at a time when it was not feasible to give it the necessary consideration before the prorogation of that short session of parliament.
Is that a reason? Does parliament have to be sitting before the government can consider these matters? Did we arrive here last January and find a draft bill ready to submit to this house for consideration? Is it necessary for the house to be sitting before emergency matters such as this can be given consideration by the government? And where is the legislation at even this late date? There is no legislation. We are waiting to see. Surely the minister will admit that his reason for delay is a lamentably weak reason for not having introduced a housing scheme. Surely the house does not have to be in
session before the matter can receive the active consideration of the minister. We did not arrive here and find any plan ready for us. The employment commission reports, and we " wait and see," while another commission reports. Meanwhile what are we doing about slum clearance? What are we doing about low cost housing? What have we done about the report submitted a year ago? What are we doing in regard to farm housing? What are we doing about the dilapidated homes in the rural areas? Soon it will be too late to do anything. As I said at the beginning, we are temporizing with results rather than dealing with causes. We are failing to tackle directly any specific problem. We pay out millions of dollars for relief and flirt flippantly with the causes that make it necessary.
We are faced with many difficult problems which the minister touched upon or brushed in his three hour speech; I have mentioned only two to-day, youth rehabilitation and housing. Much could be said of a positive nature in this regard but I have already taken a good deal of time, and I shall reserve what I have to say of a constructive nature to a later occasion. Meantime we are to " wait and see " and mark time. We must " wait " for another commission to report, and " see " what they report. Meantime what of the employable unemployed? What about those employed part time? What about untrained youth? What about dwellers in slums and dilapidated farm houses? Are they to remain neglected? Is a vast percentage of our youth to remain untrained? Must we expect those who live in farm houses that have long outlived their usefulness to continue to live under such unspeakable conditions? Will slums not be cleared? How long is the government to continue this policy of " wait and see "? There is an emergency facing this dominion which calls for something more than a three hour speech, an emergency which goes to the very quick centre of our national life; for it affects the homes of the country and those who live in them. The government, by neglecting the training of our youth deprives them not only of the opportunity to earn, but to leam how to earn. We are compelling many of those who live in our cities and on our farms to live under horrible conditions while we " wait and see."
In the name of humanity, let us away with this policy of " wait and see."
Progress reported.
